title: Contracts Instead of Trust
author: Aaron M. Renn
summary: Aaron Renn uses the restoration of Detroit's Basilica of St. Anne, where the Pulte family foundation funded $50 million on condition that the archdiocese transfer ownership to a donor-controlled nonprofit and lease the church back for $1 a year, as a window onto a broader institutional trend: legal structures replacing trust as the basis of relationships with institutions. He notes similar arrangements among evangelical donors and identifies four drivers of donor hesitancy: fear that money will be redirected to liabilities such as abuse settlements, theological drift, denominational seizure and sale of property, and 'steeplejacking' of independent congregations. Comments from Hunter Baker about external endowments for Christian colleges and a Methodist writer on conference property sales show the logic spreading. Renn's central judgment is that when devout members no longer trust their own institutions with long-lived assets, something has gone badly wrong, and that captive nonprofits only relocate or postpone the problem. His closing move is to argue that foundations are institutions too and will face the same decay, so the only real guarantor is successful generational succession to faithful, competent stewards.
points: The Detroit arrangement, a 200-year renewable lease at $1 a year from a donor-controlled nonprofit, partially reverses the Catholic Church's historic opposition to lay 'trusteeism' over property.
Renn names four reasons donors hesitate to give long-lived assets to churches: mismanagement or liability exposure, theological drift, denominational misappropriation, and steeplejacking.
The same logic is spreading to Christian higher education, with donors advised to hold endowments externally and release annual gifts only while institutions stay on mission.
Captive nonprofits substitute legal structure for lost trust but only postpone the problem, since foundations must also pass to heirs and successors and are subject to the same institutional decay.
His leadership lesson is that no governance mechanism substitutes for deliberate generational succession to faithful, competent stewards.
quotes: It’s an example of how legal structures are starting to replace trust as the basis of relationships with institutions, even churches.

This property structure is particularly notable as the Catholic Church previously fought against lay ownership and control of church property - the “trusteeism” model - so this represents a partial reversion of ownership, if not control over operations.

Denominational misappropriation. In mainline denominations, the denomination exerts significant control over local congregations and their property. Factions at denominational HQ can impose changes from above, which can lead to situations like a church building being sold off.

The fact that some of their own devout and highly committed members increasingly don’t trust churches or associated institutions enough to donate money to them for long-lived asset is a sign something is going very wrong here.

The captive non-profit is an attempt to create a legal structure to substitute for lost trust in churches. However, this only temporarily solves the problem. Eventually, even a family foundation type structure will have to pass on to heirs or successors.

Non-profits and family foundations are institutions too, and they will not be immune to the trends affecting legacy organizations like churches. Ultimately, the only genuine guarantor of institutions and property is a successful handoff to successive generations of faithful, competent stewards of them.
